title: Longest Both-Case Substring
statement:
Call a string two-faced if every letter in it appears in both its lowercase and its uppercase form. "aBbA" is two-faced; "aBb" is not, because a has no A.

Given a string s of English letters, return its longest substring (a contiguous piece) that is two-faced. If several have the same longest length, return the one that starts earliest. If there is none, return the empty string.

How many times each form appears does not matter, only that both appear.

examples.why: "Zz" is also two-faced but shorter. Any piece containing a q fails, since there is no Q.
"dD" and "Ee" tie at length 2; "dD" starts first.
Two lowercase k and one uppercase K is fine. The J has no j, so it is left out.

hints: Start with brute force: check every substring. With two bitmasks (lowercase seen, uppercase seen) you can extend a substring by one character in O(1).
A letter that appears in only one case in the whole string can never be part of an answer. What does that do to the string?

Such a letter cuts the string into pieces, and the answer lies entirely inside one piece. Recurse on each piece. Or: fix the number of distinct letters t from 1 to 26 and slide a window that holds at most t of them.

explain.intuition:
Look at the whole string first. If some character's other case appears nowhere in it, no two-faced substring can contain that character. So it acts as a wall: the answer lives entirely to its left or entirely to its right. Split there and solve both sides. If no such wall exists, the whole string is two-faced and is the answer. Each split removes at least one letter from the set of usable letters in a piece, so the recursion is at most 26 levels deep.

A sliding window also works if you fix how many distinct letters (ignoring case) the answer has. For each t from 1 to 26, move the right end forward and shrink from the left whenever the window holds more than t distinct letters. A window with exactly t letters, all in both cases, is a candidate. The longest answer is always found this way, because a longer window with the same letters would also be two-faced.
steps: If the string has fewer than 2 characters, return "".
Put all its characters in a set.
Scan for the first character whose other case is not in the set. If there is none, return the whole string.
Otherwise solve the part before it and the part after it recursively.
Return the longer result, preferring the left one on a tie so the earliest start wins.
pitfalls: Requiring equal counts of lowercase and uppercase. "kKk" is two-faced.
Taking the right part on a tie. The left part starts earlier and must win.
Checking the wall against the original full string instead of the current piece. Inside a piece, a letter's partner may have been cut off.

complexity.time: O(26 · n) for divide and conquer and for the windows

solutions.title: Every substring with bitmasks
solutions.idea: For each start, extend to the right while tracking which lowercase and which uppercase letters were seen. The substring is two-faced when the two masks are equal.

solutions.title: Divide and conquer at unusable letters
solutions.idea: A character whose other case is missing from the current piece can never be in the answer, so split around it.

solutions.title: Sliding window per number of distinct letters
solutions.idea: For each t from 1 to 26, keep the longest window ending at r with at most t distinct letters, and test whether it has exactly t letters, each in both cases.

followups: Return the number of two-faced substrings instead of the longest one.
The same split-at-a-wall idea solves "longest substring where every character appears at least k times". Why does the wall argument still hold there?
